demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
**Patient Vignette: "Mr. A."**

Mr. A. is a 62-year-old married man of European descent who has worked as a bank teller for the past thirty-four years. He presents as a slender, neatly dressed man who sits forward in his chair, his hands clasped tightly in his lap. He speaks in a low, measured tone, often pausing to look at the floor before continuing. He has been married to his wife, Carol, for thirty-nine years, and they have two adult children who live out of state.

The event that changed everything occurred fourteen months ago, on a wet Tuesday afternoon in November. Mr. A. was driving home from work, taking his usual route through a residential neighborhood. He remembers the rain was heavy, the kind that makes the windshield blur no matter how fast the wipers move. He was stopped at a red light, and when it turned green, he proceeded through the intersection. He did not see the man. The pedestrian was wearing a dark coat, and according to the police report, he stepped out from between two parked cars, directly into Mr. A.’s path. Mr. A. hit him at approximately twenty-five miles per hour.

The man survived, but with catastrophic injuries. He suffered a traumatic brain injury, multiple fractures, and internal bleeding. He spent six months in a rehabilitation facility and now lives in a long-term care home, requiring around-the-clock assistance. Mr. A. knows this because he has looked up the man’s name online, found the GoFundMe page his family set up, and read every update. He has never contacted them. He does not know what he would say.

In the months immediately following the accident, Mr. A. could not drive. He took the bus, which added an hour to his commute each way. When he finally forced himself back behind the wheel, he found he could only drive on residential streets at less than twenty miles per hour, his eyes darting to every shadow, every parked car, every pedestrian. He now takes a longer, less direct route to work that avoids intersections. He leaves his house forty-five minutes early to account for the detour.

At the bank, Mr. A. has become hypervigilant in ways he cannot control. He counts and recounts the cash in his drawer three or four times before closing. He checks the locks on the vault door repeatedly, sometimes getting up from his desk to verify a lock he already confirmed. His supervisor has noticed, and last month, Mr. A. was gently asked if he was feeling okay. He said he was fine. He is not fine.

The nightmares began about three weeks after the accident. They are not always the same, but they always end the same way: the impact, the sound, the sudden stop. Sometimes in the dream, the man is his son. Sometimes it is his wife. Sometimes it is a stranger whose face he cannot see, but whose weight he feels against the front of his car. He wakes up gasping, covered in sweat, his heart pounding so hard he thinks he might be having a heart attack. Carol has learned not to touch him when he wakes up, because he flinches away.

He has stopped going to the grocery store. He cannot bear the aisles, the people moving unpredictably, the sudden turns. He has stopped attending his grandson’s soccer games because the parking lot is too chaotic. He tells his family he is just tired, getting older. He tells himself the same thing.

At his last physical, his blood pressure was dangerously high. His doctor prescribed a beta-blocker and suggested he see a therapist. Mr. A. filled the prescription but did not follow up on the therapy referral until his wife, Carol, found him sitting in the dark in the living room at 3:00 AM, staring at the wall. She did not yell. She simply sat beside him and held his hand. The next morning, she made the appointment for him.

Mr. A. is not sure why he is here. He says he does not feel like he deserves to feel better. He says he knows it was an accident, but that does not change what he did. He carries the weight of that moment with him constantly, a stone in his chest that grows heavier with each passing day. He is a man who has spent his entire life following rules, being careful, doing things the right way, and now he has broken the one rule that cannot be fixed: he hurt someone, and he cannot take it back.
